lesson.title: CSMA: Listen Before You Talk
lesson.summary: Carrier Sense Multiple Access improves on ALOHA by having a station listen to the shared medium and defer transmission if it hears another signal already in progress, sharply reducing, though never eliminating, the rate of collisions caused by simultaneous transmission.
lesson.body:
ALOHA's central weakness is that a station transmits with no idea whether the channel is already busy. Carrier Sense Multiple Access, CSMA, fixes the obvious part of that problem: before transmitting, a station first senses the medium, checking whether a carrier signal, someone else's ongoing transmission, is currently present. This one change, listen before you talk, is why CSMA reliably outperforms ALOHA's blind transmission under most traffic conditions, since a huge share of ALOHA's collisions come from a station transmitting into a channel that was already carrying another frame the entire time.

What a station does when it finds the channel busy defines the specific CSMA variant. In 1-persistent CSMA, the station keeps sensing continuously and transmits the instant the channel goes idle, transmitting with probability 1 as soon as it can. This is simple but means that if two stations are both waiting for the same busy channel to free up, they are almost guaranteed to collide the moment it does. In non-persistent CSMA, a station that finds the channel busy does not wait right at the edge of idleness. Instead it waits a random amount of time and then senses again, which reduces collisions at the cost of leaving the channel idle a bit longer than necessary even when no one is waiting to send. p-persistent CSMA, typically used on slotted channels, splits the difference: when the channel is idle, the station transmits with probability p and defers to the next slot with probability 1 minus p, so tuning p lets a network trade off between aggressiveness and collision rate.

Even with perfect carrier sensing, CSMA cannot eliminate collisions, because sensing is not instantaneous relative to the medium's propagation delay. Consider two stations, A and B, at opposite ends of a shared cable, with one way propagation delay Tp between them. If A begins transmitting at time 0, that signal does not physically reach B until time Tp. If B happens to check the channel and finds it idle at any time before Tp, because A's signal has not arrived yet, B will also start transmitting, and the two signals will collide somewhere on the cable. This gap, the propagation delay, is why CSMA collisions are still possible, and why the ratio of propagation delay to frame transmission time is such a critical parameter for how well CSMA performs: a small Tp relative to frame time makes collisions rare, while a large Tp, from a long cable or short frames, makes them common.

CSMA on its own only handles avoidance before the fact. It says nothing about what happens once a collision does occur beyond the fact that, exactly as in ALOHA, both transmissions are corrupted and both senders will eventually notice via missing acknowledgments and retransmit after a random backoff. Two further refinements built directly on top of CSMA close that gap in ways suited to different physical media: CSMA with collision detection stops a colliding transmission early on a wired shared medium where detecting an in-progress collision is physically possible, and CSMA with collision avoidance uses explicit signaling to prevent collisions before they happen on wireless media where mid transmission detection generally is not possible.
